claim: Genome-wide association studies have revealed >270 loci associated with schizophrenia risk.
source: Genome-wide association studies have revealed >270 loci associated with schizophrenia risk, yet these genetic factors do not seem to be sufficient to fully explain the molecular determinants behind this psychiatric condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published GWAS studies (Farrell et al., 2015; Trubetskoy et al., 2022) mentioned in the Introduction section.

claim: Genetic factors do not seem to be sufficient to fully explain the molecular determinants behind schizophrenia.
source: Genome-wide association studies have revealed >270 loci associated with schizophrenia risk, yet these genetic factors do not seem to be sufficient to fully explain the molecular determinants behind this psychiatric condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that most genetic variants are in non-coding regions and the incomplete heritability of schizophrenia.

claim: Epigenetic marks such as post-translational histone modifications remain largely plastic during development and adulthood.
source: Epigenetic marks such as post-translational histone modifications remain largely plastic during development and adulthood, allowing a dynamic impact of environmental factors, including antipsychotic medications, on access to genes and regulatory elements.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about epigenetic mechanisms and their plasticity.

claim: Environmental factors, including antipsychotic medications, can dynamically impact access to genes and regulatory elements.
source: Epigenetic marks such as post-translational histone modifications remain largely plastic during development and adulthood, allowing a dynamic impact of environmental factors, including antipsychotic medications, on access to genes and regulatory elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the plasticity of epigenetic marks and established knowledge about environmental influences on gene regulation.

claim: Few studies have profiled cell-specific genome-wide histone modifications in postmortem brain samples from schizophrenia subjects.
source: However, few studies so far have profiled cell-specific genome-wide histone modifications in postmortem brain samples from schizophrenia subjects, or the effect of antipsychotic treatment on such epigenetic marks.
evidence: This is supported by the literature review presented in the Introduction section.

claim: The study conducted ChIP-seq analyses focusing on histone marks H3K27ac and H3K4me3 in frontal cortex samples from schizophrenia subjects and controls.
source: Here, we conducted ChIP-seq analyses focusing on histone marks indicative of active enhancers (H3K27ac) and active promoters (H3K4me3), alongside RNA-seq, using frontal cortex samples from antipsychotic-free (AF) and antipsychotic-treated (AT) individuals with schizophrenia, as well as individually matched controls (n=58).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Abstract and supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: H3K27ac marks active enhancers.
source: Here, we conducted ChIP-seq analyses focusing on histone marks indicative of active enhancers (H3K27ac) and active promoters (H3K4me3), alongside RNA-seq, using frontal cortex samples from antipsychotic-free (AF) and antipsychotic-treated (AT) individuals with schizophrenia, as well as individually matched controls (n=58).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Creyghton et al., 2010 in the Introduction section.

claim: H3K4me3 marks active promoters.
source: Here, we conducted ChIP-seq analyses focusing on histone marks indicative of active enhancers (H3K27ac) and active promoters (H3K4me3), alongside RNA-seq, using frontal cortex samples from antipsychotic-free (AF) and antipsychotic-treated (AT) individuals with schizophrenia, as well as individually matched controls (n=58).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bernstein et al., 2005 in the Introduction section.

claim: The study included 58 brain samples (29 schizophrenia and 29 controls).
source: Here, we conducted ChIP-seq analyses focusing on histone marks indicative of active enhancers (H3K27ac) and active promoters (H3K4me3), alongside RNA-seq, using frontal cortex samples from antipsychotic-free (AF) and antipsychotic-treated (AT) individuals with schizophrenia, as well as individually matched controls (n=58).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Abstract and confirmed in the Results section.

claim: Schizophrenia subjects exhibited thousands of neuronal and non-neuronal epigenetic differences at regions that included several susceptibility genetic loci, such as NRG1, DISC1, and DRD3.
source: Schizophrenia subjects exhibited thousands of neuronal and non-neuronal epigenetic differences at regions that included several susceptibility genetic loci, such as NRG1, DISC1, and DRD3.
evidence: This is supported by the differential analysis data presented in Figure 2 and related text.

claim: The study identified schizophrenia-associated alterations in specific transcription factors that were reversed by antipsychotic treatment.
source: By analyzing the AF and AT cohorts separately, we identified schizophrenia-associated alterations in specific transcription factors, their regulatees, and epigenomic and transcriptomic features that were reversed by antipsychotic treatment; as well as those that represented a consequence of antipsychotic medication rather than a hallmark of schizophrenia in postmortem human brain samples.
evidence: This is supported by the Taiji analysis and data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The study identified alterations that represented a consequence of antipsychotic medication rather than a hallmark of schizophrenia.
source: By analyzing the AF and AT cohorts separately, we identified schizophrenia-associated alterations in specific transcription factors, their regulatees, and epigenomic and transcriptomic features that were reversed by antipsychotic treatment; as well as those that represented a consequence of antipsychotic medication rather than a hallmark of schizophrenia in postmortem human brain samples.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis between AF and AT cohorts presented in Figure 5.

claim: The effect of age on epigenomic landscapes was more pronounced in frontal cortex of AT-schizophrenics, as compared to AF-schizophrenics and controls.
source: Notably, we also found that the effect of age on epigenomic landscapes was more pronounced in frontal cortex of AT-schizophrenics, as compared to AF-schizophrenics and controls.
evidence: This is supported by the age correlation analysis presented in Figure 7.

claim: Schizophrenia has heritability rates estimated at ~73%.
source: Schizophrenia has traditionally been viewed as a genetic disorder, with heritability rates estimated at ~73% (Sawa and Snyder, 2002; Freedman, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sawa and Snyder, 2002 and Freedman, 2003.

claim: The first GWAS study identified 108 loci associated with schizophrenia risk.
source: However, previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) clearly showed a relatively low number of genetic regions associated with schizophrenia risk – these include 108 loci in the first study (Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2014) that have been expanded to over 270 regions (Farrell et al., 2015; Trubetskoy et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2014.

claim: Most genetic variants associated with schizophrenia are located in non-coding regions.
source: Most of these genetic variants were located in non-coding regions and hence, with a few exceptions there is little evidence supporting that coding variants contribute to schizophrenia risk, which also suggests that genetic factors do not seem to be sufficient to fully explain the molecular causes underlying this severe psychiatric condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on GWAS data cited in the manuscript.

claim: Monozygotic twins have a probandwise concordance rate of 33% for schizophrenia.
source: Thus, it had originally been suggested that monozygotic twins, whose DNA sequences are approximately 100% identical, have a concordance for schizophrenia of nearly 50% (Cardno and Gottesman, 2000; Hallmayer et al., 2011), yet recent research has revealed a probandwise concordance rate of 33% in monozygotic twins and 7% in dizygotic twins (Hilker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hilker et al., 2018.

claim: Dizygotic twins have a probandwise concordance rate of 7% for schizophrenia.
source: Thus, it had originally been suggested that monozygotic twins, whose DNA sequences are approximately 100% identical, have a concordance for schizophrenia of nearly 50% (Cardno and Gottesman, 2000; Hallmayer et al., 2011), yet recent research has revealed a probandwise concordance rate of 33% in monozygotic twins and 7% in dizygotic twins (Hilker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hilker et al., 2018.

claim: Environmental factors contribute to schizophrenia susceptibility.
source: While these findings underscore the substantial influence of genetic factors on the etiology of schizophrenia, they also advocate for a significant involvement of environmental events in the intricate development of this complex disorder (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by twin study data and citation to Li et al., 2021.

claim: Prenatal maternal infection increases the risk of schizophrenia in the offspring.
source: This concept is further supported by epidemiological studies suggesting that prenatal environmental insults, such as maternal infection (Brown et al., 2004; Yudofsky, 2009) and severe adverse life events (Malaspina et al., 2008), increase the risk of schizophrenia in the offspring.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2004 and Yudofsky, 2009.

claim: Severe adverse life events increase the risk of schizophrenia in the offspring.
source: This concept is further supported by epidemiological studies suggesting that prenatal environmental insults, such as maternal infection (Brown et al., 2004; Yudofsky, 2009) and severe adverse life events (Malaspina et al., 2008), increase the risk of schizophrenia in the offspring.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malaspina et al., 2008.

claim: Chromatin organization depends on epigenetic factors such as DNA methylation and histone modifications.
source: The status of chromatin organization depends on epigenetic factors, such as DNA methylation and histone modifications that primarily occur on amino-terminal tails (Gräff and Tsai, 2013; Onuchic et al., 2018; Bastle and Maze, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gräff and Tsai, 2013; Onuchic et al., 2018; Bastle and Maze, 2019.

claim: Epigenetic mechanisms lead to stable changes in gene expression without modification of DNA sequence.
source: Hence, these epigenetic mechanisms lead to stable changes in gene expression that are mediated via altered chromatin structure without modification of DNA sequence, and remain largely plastic throughout all periods of brain development and aging.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about epigenetic mechanisms.

claim: Previous studies reported alterations in chromatin structure and accessibility in tissue samples from schizophrenic subjects and controls.
source: Supporting this concept, previous studies reported alterations in chromatin structure and accessibility in tissue samples from schizophrenic subjects and controls.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies mentioned in the Introduction.

claim: Most previous reports on chromatin alterations in schizophrenia were focused on DNA methylation differences in peripheral blood and brain.
source: Most of these previous reports, however, were focused on DNA methylation differences in peripheral blood (Aberg et al., 2014) and brain (Jaffe et al., 2016; Mendizabal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aberg et al., 2014; Jaffe et al., 2016; Mendizabal et al., 2019.

claim: Only a few differences in chromatin accessibility were observed between schizophrenia subjects and controls using ATAC-seq in bulk tissue homogenates.
source: Using the assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (ATAC-seq) in bulk tissue homogenates of postmortem frontal cortex samples, only a few differences in chromatin accessibility were observed between schizophrenia subjects and controls, in contrast to thousands of age-related differential accessible chromatin regions (Bryois et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bryois et al., 2018.

claim: Enhancers are highly dynamic cis-regulatory elements with known involvement in neurodevelopmental processes.
source: Enhancers are highly dynamic cis-regulatory elements with known involvement in neurodevelopmental processes (Won et al., 2019), and the dynamics of promoters are also significantly connected with the genetic risk of certain psychiatric conditions (Dincer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Won et al., 2019.

claim: The dynamics of promoters are significantly connected with the genetic risk of certain psychiatric conditions.
source: Enhancers are highly dynamic cis-regulatory elements with known involvement in neurodevelopmental processes (Won et al., 2019), and the dynamics of promoters are also significantly connected with the genetic risk of certain psychiatric conditions (Dincer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dincer et al., 2015.

claim: Previous work combined FACS of neuronal and non-neuronal cell nuclei with ChIP-seq assays in prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex from postmortem brain samples.
source: As an example, recent work combined fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) of neuronal and non-neuronal cell nuclei with chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) assays in two brain regions (prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex) from postmortem brain samples of subjects without any known neurological or psychiatric disease (Girdhar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Girdhar et al., 2018.

claim: Strong specific enrichments occurred with schizophrenia in both H3K27ac and H3K4me3 peaks, almost exclusively in neuronal chromatin.
source: Besides the identification of cell and region-specific histone modification landscapes in this cohort of control subjects, these findings also compared their datasets with previous GWAS of individuals with psychiatric conditions, reporting that strong specific enrichments occurred with schizophrenia and weaker associations with depression in both H3K27ac and H3K4me3 peaks. This correlation was almost exclusively observed in neuronal chromatin, but not in non-neuronal cell nuclei.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Girdhar et al., 2018.

claim: Recent investigation identified rare specific epigenetic variations for a set of non-coding RNA genes in cortical neurons from schizophrenia subjects.
source: More recent investigation conducting H3K27ac and H3K4me3 ChIP-seq assays in cortical neurons from schizophrenia subjects and controls has identified rare specific epigenetic variations for a set of non-coding RNA genes (Gusev et al., 2019) and chromatin domain alterations (Girdhar et al., 2022) that may contribute to the pathogenesis of schizophrenia.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gusev et al., 2019.

claim: Previous epigenomic studies in postmortem human brain samples did not address the potential effect of previous exposure to antipsychotics on the regulation of chromatin state.
source: However, these previous epigenomic studies in postmortem human brain samples did not address the potential effect of previous exposure to antipsychotics on the regulation of chromatin state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review presented in the Introduction.

claim: Repeated administration of antipsychotic medications leads to epigenetic modifications at selected gene regions in mouse and postmortem human brain samples.
source: This is particularly relevant considering that repeated administration of antipsychotic medications leads to epigenetic modifications at selected gene regions in mouse (de la Fuente Revenga et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2018) and postmortem human brain (Kurita et al., 2012; Ibi et al., 2017) samples.
evidence: This is supported by citations to de la Fuente Revenga et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2018; Kurita et al., 2012; Ibi et al., 2017.

claim: Alterations in the glia may contribute to major psychiatric disorders.
source: Similarly, whether such type of schizophrenia-associated epigenomic changes are observable in non-neuronal frontal cortex nuclei remains unexplored; even though there is evidence that alterations in the glia may contribute to major psychiatric disorders (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: Frontal cortex is a brain region involved in processes affected in schizophrenia patients, such as perception, cognition, and sensorimotor gating.
source: Frontal cortex is a brain region involved in processes affected in schizophrenia patients, such as perception, cognition, and sensorimotor gating (Andreasen et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andreasen et al., 1994.

claim: The study selected bilateral frontal cortex (Brodmann area 9) gray matter from 58 brain samples.
source: We selected bilateral frontal cortex (Brodmann area 9) gray matter from 58 brain samples (29 schizophrenia and 29 controls).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Control subjects were individually matched based on sex and age.
source: Control subjects were individually matched based on sex and age, and to a lower degree on postmortem delay (or PMD – time between death and tissue sample collection) (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Supplementary files 1 and 2.

claim: Approximately 60,000 nuclei per NeuN+ or NeuN- sample were collected for ChIP-seq and RNA-seq.
source: Nuclei were FACS-sorted using an anti-NeuN antibody as a marker of neuronal nuclei, and NeuN-positive (NeuN+) and NeuN-negative (NeuN-) nuclei (approximately 60,000 nuclei per NeuN+ or NeuN- sample) were collected for ChIP-seq (10,000 nuclei per library) and RNA-seq (6000 nuclei per library) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: MOWChIP-seq technology generated high-quality ChIP-seq data with average unique reads of ~11 million for H3K27ac and ~14 million for H3K4me3.
source: After library preparation and sequencing, our MOWChIP-seq technology generated high-quality ChIP-seq data with average unique reads of ~11 million and ~14 million on histone modifications H3K27ac and H3K4me3, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The fraction of reads in called peaks (FRiP) averaged at 17.35% for H3K27ac and 27.59% for H3K4me3.
source: MOWChIP-seq datasets have very low background noise (de la Fuente Revenga et al., 2021) with the fraction of reads in called peaks (FRiP) average at 17.35% and 27.59% for our H3K27ac and H3K4me3 profiling, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The PCR bottleneck coefficient (PBC) was 0.90 for H3K27ac and 0.92 for H3K4me3.
source: The PCR bottleneck coefficient (PBC) was calculated to measure library complexity (0.90 and 0.92 for H3K27ac and H3K4me3, respectively), which indicates that most of our ChIP-seq datasets have no or mild bottlenecking (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Highly significant pair-wise differences in molecular marker expression were observed for all markers between NeuN+ and NeuN- nuclei samples.
source: Highly significant (median p-value = 6×10–7) pair-wise differences in molecular marker expression were observed for all markers ranging from mature, functional, and synaptic neuron markers to astrocyte, oligodendrocyte, and microglial markers (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5; Supplementary file 5) – confirming neuronal and non-neuronal cell-type identities in the NeuN+ and NeuN- nuclei samples, respectively.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5, and Supplementary file 5.

claim: The study identified 107,938 consensus peaks covering ~135 Mb (4.22% of the genome) for H3K27ac in NeuN+ nuclei.
source: We identified 107,938 consensus peaks covering ~135 Mb (4.22% of the genome) for H3K27ac in NeuN+ nuclei, 71,490 consensus peaks covering ~101 Mb (3.18% of the genome) for H3K27ac in NeuN- nuclei, 13,3137 consensus peaks covering ~164 Mb (5.12% of the genome) for H3K4me3 in NeuN+ nuclei, and 100,745 consensus peaks covering ~142 Mb (4.43% of the genome) for H3K4me3 in NeuN- nuclei.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: The study identified 71,490 consensus peaks covering ~101 Mb (3.18% of the genome) for H3K27ac in NeuN- nuclei.
source: We identified 107,938 consensus peaks covering ~135 Mb (4.22% of the genome) for H3K27ac in NeuN+ nuclei, 71,490 consensus peaks covering ~101 Mb (3.18% of the genome) for H3K27ac in NeuN- nuclei, 13,3137 consensus peaks covering ~164 Mb (5.12% of the genome) for H3K4me3 in NeuN+ nuclei, and 100,745 consensus peaks covering ~142 Mb (4.43% of the genome) for H3K4me3 in NeuN- nuclei.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: The study identified 133,137 consensus peaks covering ~164 Mb (5.12% of the genome) for H3K4me3 in NeuN+ nuclei.
source: We identified 107,938 consensus peaks covering ~135 Mb (4.22% of the genome) for H3K27ac in NeuN+ nuclei, 71,490 consensus peaks covering ~101 Mb (3.18% of the genome) for H3K27ac in NeuN- nuclei, 13,3137 consensus peaks covering ~164 Mb (5.12% of the genome) for H3K4me3 in NeuN+ nuclei, and 100,745 consensus peaks covering ~142 Mb (4.43% of the genome) for H3K4me3 in NeuN- nuclei.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: The study identified 100,745 consensus peaks covering ~142 Mb (4.43% of the genome) for H3K4me3 in NeuN- nuclei.
source: We identified 107,938 consensus peaks covering ~135 Mb (4.22% of the genome) for H3K27ac in NeuN+ nuclei, 71,490 consensus peaks covering ~101 Mb (3.18% of the genome) for H3K27ac in NeuN- nuclei, 13,3137 consensus peaks covering ~164 Mb (5.12% of the genome) for H3K4me3 in NeuN+ nuclei, and 100,745 consensus peaks covering ~142 Mb (4.43% of the genome) for H3K4me3 in NeuN- nuclei.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: The analysis revealed 2,301 differential enhancers, 262 differential promoters, and 802 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in NeuN+ nuclei between schizophrenia subjects and controls.
source: Our analysis revealed 2,301 differential enhancers, 262 differential promoters, and 802 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in NeuN+ nuclei between schizophrenia subjects and controls, while 2,657 differential enhancers, 360 differential promoters, and 1,043 DEGs were discovered in NeuN- nuclei (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2A and Supplementary file 6.

claim: The analysis revealed 2,657 differential enhancers, 360 differential promoters, and 1,043 DEGs in NeuN- nuclei between schizophrenia subjects and controls.
source: Our analysis revealed 2,301 differential enhancers, 262 differential promoters, and 802 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in NeuN+ nuclei between schizophrenia subjects and controls, while 2,657 differential enhancers, 360 differential promoters, and 1,043 DEGs were discovered in NeuN- nuclei (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2A and Supplementary file 6.

claim: The schizophrenia group had varied H3K27ac/H3K4me3 levels and RNA-seq reads compared to controls at the enhancer region of NRG1 in NeuN+ nuclei.
source: We discovered that the schizophrenia group had varied H3K27ac/H3K4me3 levels and RNA-seq reads compared to controls at various loci involved in processes related to synaptic plasticity and cognitive processes or previously associated with schizophrenia risk (Farrell et al., 2015) – these included enhancer region of NRG1 (Neuregulin 1) in NeuN+ nuclei, enhancer region of GRM3 (Metabotropic glutamate 3 receptor) in NeuN- nuclei, promoter region of DRD3 (Dopamine D3 receptor) in NeuN+ nuclei, promoter region of DISC1 in NeuN- nuclei, CDK5 (Cyclin-dependent kinase 5) mRNA in NeuN+ nuclei, and GRIN2A (Glutamate ionotropic receptor NMDA type subunit 2 A) mRNA in NeuN- nuclei (Figure 2B and C; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2B and C and Supplementary file 6.

claim: The schizophrenia group had varied H3K27ac/H3K4me3 levels and RNA-seq reads compared to controls at the enhancer region of GRM3 in NeuN- nuclei.
source: We discovered that the schizophrenia group had varied H3K27ac/H3K4me3 levels and RNA-seq reads compared to controls at various loci involved in processes related to synaptic plasticity and cognitive processes or previously associated with schizophrenia risk (Farrell et al., 2015) – these included enhancer region of NRG1 (Neuregulin 1) in NeuN+ nuclei, enhancer region of GRM3 (Metabotropic glutamate 3 receptor) in NeuN- nuclei, promoter region of DRD3 (Dopamine D3 receptor) in NeuN+ nuclei, promoter region of DISC1 in NeuN- nuclei, CDK5 (Cyclin-dependent kinase 5) mRNA in NeuN+ nuclei, and GRIN2A (Glutamate ionotropic receptor NMDA type subunit 2 A) mRNA in NeuN- nuclei (Figure 2B and C; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2B and C and Supplementary file 6.

claim: The schizophrenia group had varied H3K27ac/H3K4me3 levels and RNA-seq reads compared to controls at the promoter region of DRD3 in NeuN+ nuclei.
source: We discovered that the schizophrenia group had varied H3K27ac/H3K4me3 levels and RNA-seq reads compared to controls at various loci involved in processes related to synaptic plasticity and cognitive processes or previously associated with schizophrenia risk (Farrell et al., 2015) – these included enhancer region of NRG1 (Neuregulin 1) in NeuN+ nuclei, enhancer region of GRM3 (Metabotropic glutamate 3 receptor) in NeuN- nuclei, promoter region of DRD3 (Dopamine D3 receptor) in NeuN+ nuclei, promoter region of DISC1 in NeuN- nuclei, CDK5 (Cyclin-dependent kinase 5) mRNA in NeuN+ nuclei, and GRIN2A (Glutamate ionotropic receptor NMDA type subunit 2 A) mRNA in NeuN- nuclei (Figure 2B and C; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2B and C and Supplementary file 6.

claim: The schizophrenia group had varied H3K27ac/H3K4me3 levels and RNA-seq reads compared to controls at the promoter region of DISC1 in NeuN- nuclei.
source: We discovered that the schizophrenia group had varied H3K27ac/H3K4me3 levels and RNA-seq reads compared to controls at various loci involved in processes related to synaptic plasticity and cognitive processes or previously associated with schizophrenia risk (Farrell et al., 2015) – these included enhancer region of NRG1 (Neuregulin 1) in NeuN+ nuclei, enhancer region of GRM3 (Metabotropic glutamate 3 receptor) in NeuN- nuclei, promoter region of DRD3 (Dopamine D3 receptor) in NeuN+ nuclei, promoter region of DISC1 in NeuN- nuclei, CDK5 (Cyclin-dependent kinase 5) mRNA in NeuN+ nuclei, and GRIN2A (Glutamate ionotropic receptor NMDA type subunit 2 A) mRNA in NeuN- nuclei (Figure 2B and C; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2B and C and Supplementary file 6.

claim: Schizophrenia was the most significantly enriched trait for all the differential enhancer and promoter regions in NeuN+ and NeuN- fractions.
source: Schizophrenia was the most significantly enriched trait for all the differential enhancer and promoter regions in NeuN+ and NeuN- fractions (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Supplementary file 7.

claim: The level of enrichment was higher in differential enhancers as compared to promoters, and the highest in differential enhancers of NeuN+ nuclei.
source: Additionally, the level of enrichment was higher in differential enhancers as compared to promoters, and the highest in differential enhancers of NeuN+ nuclei (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Supplementary file 7.

claim: 236 out of 802 DEGs in NeuN+ nuclei were also identified in a previous single-nucleus RNA sequencing study in the postmortem prefrontal cortex of schizophrenics and controls.
source: Importantly, 236 out of our 802 DEGs (p-value = 1.96×10–11) in NeuN+ nuclei, and 63 out of our 1,043 DEGs (p-value = 4.18×10–6) in NeuN- nuclei were also identified in this previous single-cell dissection work.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by comparison with Ruzicka et al., 2020.

claim: 63 out of 1,043 DEGs in NeuN- nuclei were also identified in a previous single-nucleus RNA sequencing study in the postmortem prefrontal cortex of schizophrenics and controls.
source: Importantly, 236 out of our 802 DEGs (p-value = 1.96×10–11) in NeuN+ nuclei, and 63 out of our 1,043 DEGs (p-value = 4.18×10–6) in NeuN- nuclei were also identified in this previous single-cell dissection work.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by comparison with Ruzicka et al., 2020.

claim: 66 genes were identified in both the DEGs from RNA-seq and differential enhancers/promoters associated genes in NeuN+ nuclei.
source: We found that 66 (p-value = 9×10–3) and 148 (p-value = 1.7×10–2) genes were identified in both the DEGs from RNA-seq and differential enhancers/promoters associated genes in NeuN+ and NeuN- nuclei, respectively.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: 148 genes were identified in both the DEGs from RNA-seq and differential enhancers/promoters associated genes in NeuN- nuclei.
source: We found that 66 (p-value = 9×10–3) and 148 (p-value = 1.7×10–2) genes were identified in both the DEGs from RNA-seq and differential enhancers/promoters associated genes in NeuN+ and NeuN- nuclei, respectively.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: EpiSig analysis grouped 85,462 signal-enriched regions into 814 epigenomic clusters covering 14.53% of the genome.
source: For integrative analysis of these diverse epigenomic and transcriptomic data, we next employed an unbiased method called EpiSig (Ai et al., 2018), which combines the epigenomic and transcriptomic dataset into a single analysis to cluster regions with similar epigenomic profiles across all the NeuN+ and NeuN- nuclei samples. 85,462 signal-enriched regions were grouped into 814 epigenomic clusters covering 14.53% of the genome.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: The 814 epigenomic clusters were further combined into 6 groups (sections) using the K-means method.
source: These clusters were further combined into 6 groups (sections) using the K-means method (Figure 3A and B; Supplementary files 10 and 11).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3A and B.

claim: The top five Section II clusters had schizophrenia-positive association in genes enriched in GO terms 'Trans-synaptic signaling'.
source: The top five Section II clusters had schizophrenia-positive association (i.e. activity and expression schizophrenia >controls) in genes enriched in GO terms 'Trans-synaptic signaling' (FDR 4.66×10–2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Top differentially enriched cluster genes in Section III were enriched in the GO term 'Amyloid fibril formation' and were negatively associated with schizophrenia in NeuN+ nuclei.
source: Top differentially enriched cluster genes, enriched in the GO term 'Amyloid fibril formation' (FDR 5.99×10–2), were found to be negatively associated with schizophrenia in NeuN+ nuclei, whereas genes enriched in the GO term 'Neuron projection development' (FDR 3.19×10–2) were positively associated with schizophrenia in NeuN- nuclei (Figure 3A and B; Supplementary files 10 and 11).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3A and B.

claim: Genes enriched in the GO term 'Neuron projection development' were positively associated with schizophrenia in NeuN- nuclei.
source: Top differentially enriched cluster genes, enriched in the GO term 'Amyloid fibril formation' (FDR 5.99×10–2), were found to be negatively associated with schizophrenia in NeuN+ nuclei, whereas genes enriched in the GO term 'Neuron projection development' (FDR 3.19×10–2) were positively associated with schizophrenia in NeuN- nuclei (Figure 3A and B; Supplementary files 10 and 11).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3A and B.

claim: The Taiji algorithm constructed 116 individual transcriptional networks in neuronal and glial nuclei from schizophrenia subjects and controls.
source: Using the recently developed Taiji algorithm (Zhang et al., 2019), which allows access to information pertaining to transcriptional cascades deriving from upstream drivers through specific pathway mechanisms to downstream effects, we integrated epigenomic and transcriptomic data to construct 116 individual transcriptional networks in neuronal and glial nuclei from schizophrenia subjects and controls.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: All top 10 TFs of NeuN+ nuclei were found to be cell-type specific.
source: Of the top 10 TFs of NeuN+ nuclei, all were found to be cell-type specific.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: 207 regulatees were regulated by three or more TFs and were involved in processes such as 'Neurexins and neuroligins' and 'Protein-protein interactions at synapses' in NeuN+ nuclei.
source: Using the top four TFs, we identified 207 regulatees the were regulated by three or more TFs and found they were involved in processes such as 'Neurexins and neuroligins' (FDR 2.18×10–7) and 'Protein-protein interactions at synapses' (FDR 1.22×10–6) (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: All top 10 TFs of NeuN- nuclei were cell-type specific TFs.

claim: The study provides epigenomic signatures that distinguish between those observed in AF-schizophrenia subjects as well as alterations that denote previous treatment with antipsychotic medications.

evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Transcriptional mechanisms via novel pathways that had not been previously associated with schizophrenia show alterations in AF-schizophrenia subjects.
source: This integrative analysis of transcriptomic and epigenomic data at the systems level uncovered key regulators and important pathways based on their global importance in the genetic networks. We found that transcriptional mechanisms via novel pathways that had not been previously associated with schizophrenia show alterations in AF-schizophrenia subjects, and that these schizophrenia-linked pathways were statistically unaffected in the AT-schizophrenia group, consistent with a potential role of these epigenomic signatures in the clinical efficacy of antipsychotics.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion section supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Schizophrenia-linked pathways were statistically unaffected in the AT-schizophrenia group, consistent with a potential role of these epigenomic signatures in the clinical efficacy of antipsychotics.
